name: Bee venom (apitoxin)
short: Anaphylaxis and deaths reported with bee venom therapy, including live bee stings. In trials, injected bee venom acupuncture had 3.6 times the adverse-event risk of saline; skin reactions most common.
text: Bee venom is used by injection or application at acupuncture points (bee venom acupuncture), as live bee stings, and applied to the skin in ointments, gels and cosmetics. A systematic review of 145 clinical studies found adverse events ranging from skin reactions that usually resolve over several days to life-threatening anaphylaxis; in the randomised trials, bee venom acupuncture had a 3.61-fold relative risk of adverse events compared with saline injection (which the reviewers said might be over- or underestimated because of poor reporting), and they concluded that adverse events related to bee venom therapy are frequent. A systematic review of 49 studies estimated the incidence of anaphylaxis with bee venom acupuncture at 0.045% overall; the estimate was 0.083% in women and 0.019% in men, but the abstract reports no test of that difference and the two confidence intervals overlap, and there was no significant difference between patients who had been skin-tested and those with no skin-test information. A review of bee venom acupuncture states that bee venom can cause anaphylaxis and that several deaths have been reported in patients who had previously received the therapy successfully, while the overall incidence of adverse events is unknown and the number of published reports of toxicity is small; a further report, available only as a title, describes a death due to live bee acupuncture. In a systematic review of 12 randomised trials using bee venom as acupuncture injections, ultrasound gel or ointment, six trials reported adverse events, most commonly skin reactions such as itching and swelling. Case reports describe liver toxicity with progressive jaundice in a 35-year-old woman three weeks after bee sting therapy for multiple sclerosis (she later improved), in a report whose background notes that multiple stings are known to cause destruction of red blood cells (haemolysis), kidney injury, liver toxicity and heart attack; and, by title only, bleeding in the brain after multiple honeybee stings given as apitherapy; a review of cosmetic uses notes that skin reactions to bee venom can extend to excessive immune responses, including anaphylaxis. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
